analysis.one_liner: Requires mechanical logging treatment on 7.5 million acres of national forest while trimming environmental review and court challenges.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 2014, got a single Senate committee hearing, and died in committee without a vote when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Forest Service to mechanically treat — essentially log — at least 7.5 million acres of national forest land designated for timber production over 15 years, using timber sale contracts as the main tool. It would have narrowed environmental review of each project to a short assessment with just one alternative, limited public objections to a special administrative process, and replaced the right to sue in court with a binding arbitration program whose decisions could not be reviewed by any judge. Money from the projects would have been split: 25 percent to local counties, most of the rest to Forest Service reforestation and salvage funds. The bill never got a Senate vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, timber and wood products companies would have gained a guaranteed, predictable federal wood supply for 15 years, with timber sale contracts as the primary contracting method. Rural counties in timber states would have received 25 percent of project revenue on top of existing payments, and timber workers and mills in areas west of the 100th meridian would have seen more federal timber available to harvest and process.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Timber companies and rural timber counties

how_it_helps.text: It directs the Forest Service to mechanically treat at least 7.5 million acres of timber-designated national forest land over 15 years, aimed at creating a predictable wood supply to preserve and create timber jobs.
It sends 25 percent of the money the government collects from each project to the counties where the work happens, on top of existing forest revenue payments counties receive.

It limits environmental analysis to one assessment per project with a single alternative, a 100-page cap and a 180-day deadline, and requires administrative objections to go through a streamlined Healthy Forests Restoration Act process — designed to cut the cost and delay of planning timber projects.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary Americans who own the national forests would have borne the cost: less thorough environmental review (one alternative, a 100-page cap, a 180-day deadline), no route to challenge a project in court for 15 years, and a hard acreage quota that could push logging volume ahead of site-specific ecological judgment. Any remaining project revenue would have gone to the Treasury, but the main public cost was reduced oversight of logging on public land.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through reduced review of federal logging

drawbacks.text: The bill replaces ordinary judicial review with a binding arbitration pilot that would be the sole way to challenge a covered project for 15 years; the arbitrator's decision 'shall not be subject to judicial review,' so courts could not second-guess it.

Environmental analysis is narrowed: each project needs only an environmental assessment limited to the proposed action and one alternative, capped at 100 pages and due within 180 days, rather than a fuller environmental impact statement with a range of alternatives.

The bill sets a hard quota of at least 7.5 million acres mechanically treated in 15 years and bars the Forest Service from reducing acres designated for timber harvest during forest plan revisions unless needed to avoid an Endangered Species Act jeopardy finding, which could push treatment volume ahead of ecological judgment.
Administrative challenges would be limited to the special Healthy Forests Restoration Act process, trimming the standard administrative objection routes the public currently has.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goals — healthier forests, rural jobs, and money for county schools and roads — are real public benefits, and active forest management can reduce wildfire risk. But the design trades away a great deal to get them: a hard 7.5-million-acre quota prioritizes volume over what any given forest needs, environmental review is narrowed to a single alternative with page and time limits, and for 15 years a person unhappy with a logging project's review could not go to court at all — only to a binding arbitration process with tight deadlines. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the bill bought industry certainty by removing the public's ability to test government logging decisions in court. A narrower bill that streamlined reviews without eliminating judicial review could have delivered many of the same benefits at lower cost to public oversight.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which held one hearing but never voted to move it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator John Barrasso introduced the bill on January 28, 2014, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
The committee held a hearing on the bill on February 6, 2014 (printed as S.Hrg. 113-349), but took no further action on it.
No version of the bill ever reached the Senate floor for a vote, and it died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
The bill's only cosponsors were two Senate Republicans; no Democrat signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: National forests kept their existing environmental review and court-challenge protections, since no quota, narrowed review, or arbitration-only challenge process took effect. Timber companies did not get the guaranteed 15-year federal wood supply the bill promised, and counties did not get the extra 25 percent revenue share.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public lands and existing environmental safeguards

for.name: John Barrasso
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it to a committee hearing.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee (chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden)
against.what_they_did: Held a single hearing on the bill on February 6, 2014, but never marked it up, voted it out, or sent it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All three Senate sponsors were Republicans and no Democrat cosponsored; the Democratic-led committee held one hearing but never advanced the bill, and it died in committee.

industries.note: The bill guarantees a large, predictable federal wood supply by requiring 7.5 million acres of mechanical treatment over 15 years and making timber sale contracts the primary tool. That certainty comes from more logging on public land with lighter environmental review and no court challenges — a benefit that runs against the public's interest in thorough oversight of its own forests.

industries.industry: Rural county governments in western timber states
industries.note: Counties where projects occur would get 25 percent of project revenue each year, on top of existing forest payments — money that often funds schools and roads. County interests here run alongside the local communities they serve.

industries.industry: Public-interest and conservation groups that challenge federal timber sales
industries.note: During the 15-year period, arbitration would be the only way to challenge a covered project, and the arbitrator's binding decision could not be reviewed by any court. Groups that rely on litigation to enforce environmental laws would lose that tool on these lands.
